activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many school pools are 25 yards or 25 meters long, called short course, while Olympic swimming races are held in 50-meter pools, called long course.
story:
Romy pulled her cap on and stared at the time taped inside her locker door: 31.4. That was her 50-meter freestyle from summer camp, and it was the fastest thing she owned.

Titan leaned over the bench between them. "What's the number for?"

"Tryout standard is 33.5," Romy said. "I'm way under."

"Then you're fine." He snapped his goggles strap. "Stop pacing."

But she kept pacing, because the pool outside the locker room door was wrong. At camp she counted her strokes per lap the whole summer, and this pool needed fewer. When she walked past the deck on the way in, the flags at the end looked closer than they should.

Titan was already at the door. "You can delegate the worrying to me if you want. I'll worry twice as hard."

"Go warm up," she said.

At tryouts, Emy-Rose came back from her 50 shaking her head. "I'm two seconds slower than my club time and I felt fast out there."

"Club where?" Romy asked.

"Riverside. Olympic pool. Fifty meters, the whole thing."

Romy stopped toweling her hair. Her camp pool had been fifty meters too. She looked at the wall clock, then at the far end of the pool, counting the lane markers the way she counted strokes.

"Mr. Bekele," she called across the deck, "is this pool 25 meters or 25 yards?"

"Twenty-five yards," he said. "Short course. The Olympic swimmers race long course, fifty meters."

Emy-Rose frowned. "So what?"

"So our times don't compare," Romy said. "My 31.4 came from a fifty-meter pool. A short course time in a pool half the size isn't the same thing at all." She turned her heat sheet over and wrote 31.4 + ? on the back. "I could be slower here and still be better. Or faster here and worse."

"Then how do you know if you make it?" Emy-Rose asked.

Romy didn't answer. The coach blew the whistle.

She dove, and the pool went by faster than any pool she knew, turns arriving sooner, walls coming at her like they'd moved. She touched, gasped, and read the board: 30.1.

Titan whooped from the fence. "You dropped a whole second!"

Romy hauled herself out, water streaming off her elbows, and stood in front of the coach with her heat sheet still in her fist.

"I need a ruling," she said. "My old time is from long course. This one's short course. You can't put them side by side."

The coach looked at her for a long moment, then at the board. "Numbers on my board are what I coach by. Top eight make the squad."

Romy stepped back into line, pulse hammering, and wrote one thing under the 30.1: no treaty until the math is fair.

Emy-Rose bumped her shoulder. "Top eight, at least?"

"Seventh," Romy said. "For now." She capped her pen and watched the clock reset to zero.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game; the Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later.
story:
The living room at Grandma's house smelled like popcorn and lemon polish, and every chair was already taken. Ariana sat on the floor between Iman and Claira, holding her bowl so the dog couldn't invade it when nobody was looking. On the screen, the pregame show flashed the logo for the big game, and next to it, in tall gold letters, stood a Roman numeral.

"Why do they use those letters instead of a regular number?" Iman asked, dipping a chip. "Like, why not just say the number?"

"Probably because it sounds fancy," Claira said. "Everything about this game is fancy."

Ariana frowned at the screen. She turned the question over the way she did with math problems, looking for the part underneath the part you could see. Roman numerals had been used for centuries, so somebody had to have chosen them on purpose, at some particular time. A choice meant there was a moment before the choice. "I think it might not have started out that way," she said slowly. "Maybe the first one didn't have a numeral at all."

Iman laughed. "That's impossible. Then how would anybody know which one it was?"

That was exactly the kind of thing Ariana wanted to check instead of argue about. She pulled out her phone, typed carefully, and scrolled past a wall of ads. Then she held up the screen. "Look. The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game." She read it out loud so Claira, who was squinting from the couch arm, could hear. "The Roman numeral was added later."

"Later," Claira repeated. "So the numbers came after the game already existed."

"Like naming a baby after it's already walking," Grandma called from the kitchen doorway, and everyone laughed.

Ariana felt the small click of a pattern fitting together. If the numbering began later, then the fancy numerals weren't the reason the game felt big and old. The game had gotten big first, and the numerals had followed, like a coat of paint on a house that was already standing. "So it's the opposite of what it looks like," she said. "It looks like the numbers made it grand. Really the game made the numbers grand."

The kickoff interrupted before anyone could answer, and the room erupted. Iman's dad stood up and knocked over the salsa, and the dog made his move, darting under the coffee table for the popcorn bowl. Ariana lifted it high and pointed at the screen, where the gold numeral gleamed over the stadium lights.

"That's my candidate for MVP," Claira said, nodding toward the dog, who had now settled on the rug with one stolen kernel.

"He didn't even get it," Ariana said, and she covered her bowl with both hands.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: A young child can drown in just a few inches of water and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath.
story:
Ryan sat on the bench closest to the old stone fountain, because the fountain was the one thing at Maple Park he did not trust. The toddler he was watching, a two-year-old named Sam, stood at the fountain's wide rim, where the water pooled no deeper than a puddle after rain. Ryan's mother had made him read the babysitting sheet from the community center before she let him take the job, and one line had stuck with him: a young child can drown in just a few inches of water, and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath. A fountain wasn't a bath, but Ryan figured the water didn't care what it was called.

"You want the sandbox instead?" Ryan asked. Sam shook his head and patted the rim.

Across the grass, Dan and Kayden waved from the basketball court. "Come play, we need a third," Dan shouted. Ryan held up the toddler's hand to show why he couldn't, and Dan shrugged and started a game with Kayden, two against one tall kid neither of them knew.

Then Ryan's phone buzzed in his pocket. It was Sam's mother, and the call was about pickup time, so it mattered. But Ryan had noticed a pattern over the last hour: every time he looked at his phone, Sam drifted a step closer to the water. He couldn't see any reason for it, so he decided to isolate the cause with a test. He counted Sam's distance from the rim, then took out the phone and pretended to read it for five seconds. When he looked up, Sam had moved two steps closer, quiet the whole time, watching the water and not watching Ryan. That settled it. Ryan picked Sam up, settled him on one hip, and answered the phone while holding him. "We're at the park by the fountain," he said. "Six o'clock, got it." Sam grabbed a fistful of Ryan's collar and put two fingers in his own mouth.

A woman came by walking a robust brown dog on a short leash. It was Ms. Whitaker, who lived two streets over from Ryan. "That fountain's part of the town's heritage, you know," she said. "A hundred years old. They rebuilt the pump twice." Ryan said that was interesting, but he kept his body between Sam and the water the whole time they talked, and when Sam leaned toward the sound of the splashing, Ryan turned so the lean pointed at the sand pile instead.

Later, when Dan and Kayden came over at the end of their game, Kayden asked why Ryan wouldn't just set Sam down by the shallow end for one minute. "Because it doesn't take a minute," Ryan said, "and it doesn't take deep water, and there wouldn't even be any splashing." He lifted Sam higher on his hip and walked toward the swings.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
At the food court table, Megan set down her tray and slid her phone across to Paige. "Look what I found last night."

On the screen was a comment Megan had written two years ago, under a photo from Paige's old birthday party, posted publicly on a page anyone could see. The comment said something silly about Paige's cousin, and there it was, third result when Megan had typed her own name into a search box, just to see.

"I searched my name as a joke," Megan said. "And this came up. I forgot I ever wrote it."

Maisie leaned over, chewing a pretzel. "How did it find you? That was ages ago."

"Mr. Koné told us once," Paige said. "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages. So if something's posted publicly, it can turn up in search results." She shrugged. "I didn't really believe him until now."

Megan felt her stomach tighten. Anyone could see it. A stranger, a future teacher, Paige's cousin herself. She had assumed deleting the comment from her memory was the same as deleting it from the world, and that assumption had been wrong. She tried to remember how to take it down, but the account belonged to a girl named Skye who had moved away, someone Megan barely knew anymore.

"Can you contact her?" Maisie asked.

Megan scrolled through her contacts. She still had Skye's number from grade four, but calling felt enormous, like admitting she had done something predatory, lurking and saying mean things where she thought nobody was watching. It hadn't felt that way at the time. It had felt like whispering.

She wrote a message instead, and read it aloud so her friends could hear it. "Hi Skye, it's Megan. This is going to sound weird, but I found a comment I left on your page from Paige's party. It was a mean joke about your cousin, and I'm sorry. Could you delete it if it's still there? Also, the party photo shows the whole front of your house and your street sign. Did you know that was public?"

She sent it, and then the three of them sat with their drinks going watery, watching the mall crowd accelerate toward the doors as a rainstorm broke outside. Megan kept checking her phone, which felt ridiculous, since Skye lived two time zones away and probably had better things to do.

Twenty minutes later the phone buzzed. "Omg I had no idea. Deleted the comment, changed the photo settings, and asked my mom to take down the one with our house number. Thank you. Also, sorry about your hair in that picture."

Megan laughed out loud and showed the girls, relief loosening her shoulders. She opened her own settings next and flipped her page to private, thumb hovering, then tapping. Across the food court, an older man at the next table looked up from his own phone, and Megan caught his eye and pulled her screen a little closer, just in case.

"New rule," Paige said, raising her cup. "Search your name before a stranger does."

Megan clinked her cup against it. "Every month."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: In tropical rainforests, the difference between day and night temperatures can be larger than the difference between the warmest and coolest months.
story:
The departures board flickered above Gate 14, and Maya spread two printed graphs across the empty seats beside her. One showed a desert: twelve months of bars so short they looked like a row of teeth, with temperatures leaping and falling like a yo-yo. The other showed a rainforest, and its bars were tall and even, month after month, like the bars of a cage. Her class project was due the day she landed, and the teacher had said the graphs had to speak for themselves.

"We're boarding in forty minutes," said Xavier, dropping into the seat across from her with his passport in his teeth. "Why do you look like the graphs insulted you?"

"Because the rainforest one is boring," Maya said. "The temperature line just lies there. Nothing happens all year." She tapped the desert graph, where the line climbed a cliff every June and slid down every December. "This one has a story. Hot season, cold season. The rainforest doesn't."

Gurnoor leaned over from the next row, headphones around her neck. "Then read the rainforest graph differently. Look at what's not on it."

"There's nothing not on it," Maya said, but she looked anyway. The line squatted between twenty-five and twenty-eight degrees, every single month. She frowned. Months were the graph's whole way of showing change, and the rainforest had none to show. Then she thought about her suitcase upstairs at check-in, where she had packed a sweater because her aunt in the rainforest had told her to, and the thought snagged. "Wait," she said slowly. "The graph shows months. But days have temperatures too. Days aren't on here."

"Go on," Gurnoor said.

"If the months are all the same, then the difference between the warmest and coolest months is tiny, like three degrees. But nights out there get cool enough that Aunt Ruth says bring a sweater. So day to night could swing more than month to month does." She pulled out her pencil and wrote it in the margin: in a tropical rainforest, day and night temperatures can differ more than the warmest and coolest months do. Then she sat back, feeling the fatigue of the early start drain out of her, replaced by something brighter.

"Boarding group two," the gate agent announced, and the line began to shuffle forward. Maya gathered her graphs, and the cold window glass made her breath condense into a small grey cloud, which vanished the way it had come. Ms. Sun, the neighbour who had driven them, waved from beyond security with her porous canvas tote bag sagging off her shoulder.

"Text me a picture of the margin note," Xavier said, hoisting his backpack. "I want to steal it."

"Then you owe me a rainforest fact in return," Maya said, and stepped into the line.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: On drawing pencils, H is usually read as 'hardness' and B as 'blackness', so a 6B pencil makes darker, softer marks than a 4H.
story:
Juliette pressed harder, and the paper still gave her almost nothing. Her shading looked like breath on a window. Across the table, Allison's portrait of Ms. Sadeghi was already rich and dark, the shadows under the eyes soft as charcoal, and the bell for cleanup was fifteen minutes away.

"Move your arm," Allison said, leaning over. "Let me see." She picked up Juliette's pencil, turned it toward the window light, and read the tiny letters stamped into the wood. "No wonder. You've got a 4H. I've been drawing with a 6B." She held her own pencil beside it. "See? B is for blackness. Yours is the H end."

Juliette turned her pencil over twice, as if the letters might rearrange themselves. H had to be the opposite, then, hardness, which was exactly what the paper kept telling her. She and Allison always split the pencil box between them, and at the start of class they had both reached in blind while arguing about who got the good seat near the window. Somewhere in that scramble, the pencils had swapped sides of the box. That was the hidden cause, and she could test it. She went back to the box, checked the slots, and found the empty 6B slot on her side, right where the 4H had been sitting in the wrong row.

The new pencil went down like dark silk. In two minutes she built a jawline, a cloud of hair, the fold of a collar. It was the best thing she had made all term, and it existed only because she'd ruined the first attempt. Emma-Rose wandered over from the clay table, where she had been trying to mediate a dispute about who had flattened someone's coil pot, and whistled at the drawing.

"Ms. Sadeghi wants these finished today," Emma-Rose said. "For the display by the office. The welcome thing for the new students."

"The refugee families," Allison said quietly. "The ones starting Monday."

Juliette looked at her half-finished portrait, at the faint ghost of the first version still visible under the new darks. There was no time to finish it now. Ms. Sadeghi came by, looked for a long moment, and said, "Leave it. I'll hang what's done. Unfinished drawings aren't immune to being beautiful." She picked it up carefully, and Juliette watched her half-dark, half-pale face travel toward the office wall, pinned among the finished ones, wearing its whole history right there for everyone to see.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: In hot deserts, the sun and dry air could evaporate far more water in a year than falls as rain, so the ground stays dry.
story:
Amelia spread the two graphs across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with salt shakers. One graph showed a hot desert, twelve bars for twelve months of rainfall, most of them so short they looked like toothpicks. The other showed a rainforest, and its bars climbed like a skyline. The temperature lines wiggled across the bottom of both pages. Her science packet said to compare them by Monday, and Ms. Cardinal had written one comment in red pen: "Tell me why, not just what."

"That's the part I don't get," Amelia muttered. The desert was hot and it did rain there, a little. So why didn't the water pile up over the years until the place turned green?

She texted Kolten, who had spent the summer with his uncle in Arizona. His reply came back in pieces: "u wont believe this." Then: "i dumped a bucket of water in the yard." Then a photo of a dark wet patch on orange dirt, with a shadow stretched long across it, early morning. "watch this," the last message said. "check back before lunch."

Amelia set her phone against the sugar bowl and stared at the graphs while the clock ticked toward noon. The desert's rainfall bars added up to only a few centimeters in a whole year. The rainforest's added up to more than two meters, and the narrator of her textbook called that the wettest climate on Earth. If rain kept landing in the desert, even a little, year after year, some of it should stay. Ponds. Mud. Something. Unless it was leaving.

The phone buzzed. Kolten had sent another photo of the same patch of dirt, and the wet spot was gone. The ground was pale and cracked, as if the bucket of water had never existed. "before lunch," his message said. "i timed it. gone."

Amelia sat very still. Something clicked, the way a lock does. Water could leave. It could rise off the ground into the air, invisible, and the desert had the two things that made it happen fast: blazing sun and dry air. The sun and dry air could evaporate far more water in a year than fell as rain in that same year. That was the hidden rule the graphs had been hiding. The rainforest got soaked because rain fell faster than it could evaporate. The desert stayed thirsty because the sky drank more than it gave.

She wrote her answer in one careful paragraph, then read it aloud to test it. "The bars are small, but the real story is what the sun and dry air take back." On Monday, Ms. Cardinal handed the packets back, and when Amelia flipped her page over, there was no red pen, only a check mark and one anonymous sticky note that had to be hers: "Now compare the temperature lines." Amelia grinned, pulled out a fresh pencil, and bent over the graphs again.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Astigmatism happens when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, which blurs vision at any distance.
story:
Logan had been pretending for weeks that the whiteboard was fine, but on Tuesday he copied the homework wrong twice, and Emmy ended up texting him the assignment both nights, which she said was "not a sustainable system." Now he was sitting in a small padded chair at the optometrist's office while the doctor's assistant flipped lenses in front of his face. Brandon had come along because his mother was dropping them at practice afterward, and he was currently entertaining himself by reading the eye chart upside down from the waiting bench. "E, F, P," he announced. "To, Z, and something that looks like a duck."

"Logan, which is better, one or two?" asked Ms. Wiśniewski, the optometrist, flipping a lens. Logan squinted. With lens two, the letters sharpened and then, strangely, smeared again, as if someone had dragged a thumb across wet ink. That was the part that had confused him for months, and he finally had a place to ask about it. "It's weird," he said. "It's blurry when I read my book and blurry when I look at the board. I thought eyes went one way or the other. Near or far."

"Reasonable guess," Ms. Wiśniewski said. "What's your next most probable theory?" Logan thought about it while she held up a card with a fan of black lines, some vertical, some horizontal. "The vertical lines are clear and the sideways ones are fuzzy," he said slowly. "So it's not about distance at all. It's about direction." He turned the card ninety degrees and the fuzziness moved with it. On the desk beside the chair sat a plastic model of an eye, and next to it a transparent shape that was round on one axis and stretched, like an egg, on the other. He picked up the egg-shaped piece and turned it in the light. "If the front of the eye is shaped like this, then it bends light more in one direction than the other. That would smear things at any distance, near or far."

"Astigmatism," Ms. Wiśniewski said, and made a note on her pad. "Read the bottom line for me." Logan read it, and it was like the whole room had been wiped clean. He had been walking around in a mild fog without knowing it, and now the exit signs, the pattern on the ceiling tiles, and Brandon's terrible upside-down chart were all in focus at once.

A week later he picked out grey frames, and when the cashier handed over the receipt he signed his name with an unnecessary flourish. "Very fancy," said Brandon. "Now you can see my tundra diorama. It's due Monday and it's mostly cotton balls." Logan slid the glasses on. Outside, the maple tree across the parking lot had individual leaves, thousands of them, each one distinct. "You should have put that many cotton balls in the tundra," he said. Brandon considered the tree. "How many is that?" Logan grinned. "Come on, we'll count them at practice."

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: If a company goes bankrupt, its bondholders must be paid back before its stockholders, who are last in line and often receive nothing.
story:
Anais spread the newspaper clipping on the kitchen table next to her cereal bowl and read it for the third time. The headline said a toy company called Tinker Toys had gone bankrupt, and her cousins Rocco and Hanna were coming over in forty minutes to argue about it before she had to leave for her violin lesson.

"You're the one who likes puzzles," her mom had said that morning, sliding the clipping across the counter. "They've been fighting about this for a week. See if you can figure out who's right."

When Rocco and Hanna arrived, they were already arguing on the front steps. Rocco held up a crumpled paper. "Grandpa gave me stock in Tinker Toys. It has to still be worth something, right? It's a real company."

Hanna waved her own paper. "He gave me a bond. Same company. So they're worth the same, obviously. It's all just paper."

Anais poured them each a glass of juice and sat down. "Okay, before I have to leave, let's be systematic about this. Same company, but stock and bond aren't the same thing." She had read that much in the encyclopedia the night before, sitting cross-legged on her bed while her mom watched TV downstairs.

"It's just a toy company," Rocco said. "Who cares?"

"You care, because you're holding the paper." Anais tapped the clipping. "It says here the company went bankrupt. That means everybody it owes money to gets in a line."

Hanna frowned. "A line? Like at the cafeteria?"

"Sort of. Grandma calls it being last in line." Anais tried to remember the exact words from the encyclopedia, the way she tried to diagnose a wrong note in her practicing, by going back to the beginning and checking each step. "If a company goes bankrupt, the bondholders must be paid back before the stockholders. Stockholders are last in line, and they often get nothing."

Rocco's face changed slowly, like milk souring. "So Hanna gets paid first?"

"And I probably get nothing at all," Rocco said, not quite asking.

"That's what last in line means," Anais said. She watched him fold his paper smaller and smaller, the way he folded wrappers when he was nervous. Hanna didn't smile. She turned her own paper over and over in her hands, as if it had suddenly grown heavier.

"So mine's worth more," Hanna said quietly. "That doesn't feel like winning."

Anais glanced at the clock. Twelve minutes until she had to leave. "You could split whatever Hanna gets," she offered. "Cousins, right?"

Rocco shrugged. "Maybe." He unfolded his paper and smoothed it flat on the table, next to Hanna's, two rectangles side by side. "Yours still says bond," he said.

"It still says bond," Hanna agreed, and she slid it an inch closer to his.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: A crescendo means gradually getting louder, and a diminuendo or decrescendo means gradually getting softer.
story:
Grandma's piano had a wobbly middle C, and Aurora loved it anyway. She had been practicing the same piece for two weeks, the one her teacher had nominated for the spring recital, and she could play every note without the sheet music. But when Grandma stopped peeling apples in the kitchen and came to stand in the doorway, Aurora knew something was still wrong.

"It sounds right," Grandma said, "but it sounds the same. Loud the whole way through, like a marching band stuck at one volume."

Aurora looked at the page. All over the margins her teacher had written strange words under curved lines, like gates opening and closing. She had ignored them, mostly, because the notes seemed more important. Now she squinted at one that said crescendo, stretched under eight measures, and another farther on that said diminuendo.

Grandma went back to her apples. The cat, Duchess, sprawled lethargic across the sunny windowsill, barely opened one eye. Aurora played the first line at full volume, then tried the eight measures starting quiet, almost whispering, and growing a little louder each bar, so that by the end the sound filled the whole room. Grandma's paring knife stopped again.

"That's it," Grandma called. "That's the shape of it."

So crescendo means gradually getting louder, Aurora thought, and it made sense of the word too, like something cresting. Then the diminuendo had to be the opposite, going gradually softer. Her friend Eva had done exactly this in band rehearsal last month, and Aurora suddenly understood why their band director had winced. The whole trumpet section had blasted the crescendo all at once, a wall of sound with no ramp, and afterward Eva said it was like being attacked by a parasite that swelled up suddenly instead of creeping in slowly. Aurora had laughed then. Now, at the piano, she got it.

She played the piece through, letting it swell where the gates opened and letting it fade where they closed. The final diminuendo was the hardest, like slowing down a bicycle without wobbling, but she kept her hands steady and drew the sound down until the last note was barely there.

In the doorway, Grandma had a plate of sliced apple in her hands. "Duchess woke up for that part," she said. "Even she could tell the ending was coming." The cat blinked at them both from the windowsill, tail curled like a treble clef.

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: Side-angle-side appears as Proposition 4 in Book I of Euclid's Elements, the ancient Greek geometry book written around 300 BCE.
story:
Mathis had written and erased the same proof four times, and his eraser was leaving grey smears across the page like shadows. The worksheet asked him to prove that two triangles were congruent, and he knew the rule had something to do with two sides and the angle between them, but every time he tried to set it out, the letters jumbled. He despised proofs that way, the way some people despise broccoli, with his whole body.

He got up to find a snack and passed the bookshelf in the hall, the one nobody ever looked at. Behind a fat cookbook stood a thin old book with a cracked spine, his grandfather's, from before the family moved. Mathis pulled it out to see what it was. The cover said Euclid's Elements in faded gold letters. He carried it back to the kitchen table out of curiosity more than hope.

He opened it near the front, where a page of diagrams showed triangles stacked like roof trusses. In Book I, the book said, Proposition 4 was illustrated with two triangles that shared the same two sides and the same angle squeezed between them. Mathis sat very still. Around 300 BCE, the page before noted, some ancient Greek geometer had written all this down. His homework rule was sitting inside a book older than almost anything he owned.

He tested it against his worksheet. He copied his triangles onto scrap paper, cut them out with the kitchen scissors, and laid one on top of the other. The cut edges matched along both sides, and the corners sat flush. It was not real proof, he knew that, but it showed him what the proof should do, so he went back and wrote it out in order: these sides equal, this angle between them equal, those sides equal. The smears stayed on the page, but the logic sat clean on top of them.

He texted Maksim a photo of the old book. "This guy figured out my homework 2300 years ago."

Maksim replied with a row of exclamation marks, then: "Bring it Monday. Danica will want a critique of the diagrams. She says the ones in our textbook look like they were drawn during an earthquake."

The next morning Mathis showed the book to Mr. Rahman at the start of math class. "Side-angle-side is Proposition 4," Mathis said, tapping the page. "In Book I. It's been in there since around 300 BCE."

Mr. Rahman turned the fragile pages carefully, the way you handle something you suspect might be influential. "And it still works," he said.

During lunch, Danica traced the diagrams onto binder paper with a sharp pencil, declared the ancient Greek lines "actually pretty good," and slid the book back across the table. Mathis tucked it into his backpack, between his binder and his lunch bag, where it rode home with him.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: When each person pays for their own share of a bill, it is often called 'going Dutch'.
story:
Chloe had forty minutes until the movie started, and she still couldn't tell whether Ocean was nervous or just hungry. He kept glancing at the food trucks like a stray dog sizing up a butcher shop, while Lilian, walking beside them with the smug patience of someone who had arranged this whole date, pretended not to notice anything at all.

"Ten minutes for snacks," Lilian announced, checking her phone. "Then we run to the theater. There's no way we're missing the previews again."

They stopped at the coffee cart near the fountain, the one with the long line and the faint smell of burnt sugar. The sun was starting to drop behind the tennis courts. When their turn came, Chloe ordered a frozen hot chocolate because it sounded like a contradiction she wanted to consume personally, and Ocean ordered lemonade, and then the moment arrived that she had been dreading. The cashier said the total. Both of them froze.

Her instinct said the boy was supposed to pay. But her allowance was exactly enough for her own drink, not two, and she couldn't read Ocean's face at all. Had he brought money? Was he waiting for her? The line behind them shifted impatiently. A little kid groaned, "Hurry uuuup," and the sound of it made everything worse, like a countdown nobody had agreed to.

Then Chloe remembered something. Her aunt had said it once at a diner, laughing, when she and her friend had each pulled out their wallets at the same time. Chloe had thought it was a boring grown-up detail then, tedious, the kind of thing adults discussed instead of anything interesting. Now it felt like a rope thrown into deep water.

"We could go Dutch," she said.

"Go what?" Ocean blinked at her.

"When each person pays for their own share of a bill," Chloe said. "It's called going Dutch."

Relief crossed his face so fast it was almost funny. "Yes. That. Please." He counted out his coins for the lemonade while Chloe paid for her frozen hot chocolate, and the cashier, mercifully, rang them up separately without commentary. Lilian, waiting by the fountain, gave a small thumbs up that she probably thought Chloe couldn't see.

They ran for the theater with their cups sweating in their hands, and Chloe decided the second date, if there was one, should definitely involve more seating and fewer deadlines. The ticket line stretched out the door and around the corner. Ocean looked at it, then at her, then at the sky darkening above the park.

"Still fifteen minutes," he said. "We can make it if we drink fast."

"Race you to the trash can," Chloe said, and tipped her cup back.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
story:
James stood in his grandmother's laundry room holding two shirts and pretending he knew what he was doing. He was there because his mother had won the argument at breakfast: he was twelve, and it was time he learned to do a load of laundry from sorting to folding. His grandmother had agreed to teach him, though so far she had mostly sat on her stool near the window and let him figure things out.

"Sort them into piles," she said. "Dark ones there, pale ones there."

He spread the laundry across the floor like a general planning an invasion of a tiny monarchy, one towel claiming the whole centre of the room. He was halfway through when he picked up his white school shirt and paused. Something about it nagged at him.

Last summer, at his cousin's house, his white shirt had come out of the wash pale pink. Nobody had spilled anything on it. At the time he'd blamed the machine, but now he stared at the red sock sitting in the dark pile, the one his grandmother had just bought him, and an idea crept in. The sock had been in that load. It was new then, too. New dark or bright clothes could let dye loose into the wash water, he reasoned, and that water could tint everything pale that shared it. He couldn't see dye floating around in there, but the pink shirt had been proof of something invisible.

He decided to test it, in a small way. He filled a bowl with warm water and dropped the new red sock in. While he waited, his grandmother handed him the measuring cup for the detergent and showed him the dial for the water level. "You're going to make a better launderer than your grandfather," she said. "He once turned all his underwear purple."

James laughed, then leaned over the bowl. The water had gone faintly pink. "Grandma, look." He lifted the sock and dropped in a scrap of white fabric from her sewing basket. When he pulled it out, it had a blush of colour, faint but real. His guess had been right, and the cause had been hiding in plain water all along.

"New red sock, separate load," he announced, writing it on a sticky note and pressing it to the machine. His grandmother said the note would still be there when he was thirty.

He ran the pale load first, carefully, checking the dial twice. While it agitated, he called Jace, who was home with a broken wrist and nothing to do. "I'm doing laundry," James said. "You can collaborate from the couch. Tell me when the timer hits twenty minutes." When the load finished, he hauled the heavy wet clothes to the line, pinned them up, and later took them down warm and stiff from the sun. He folded the school shirt on the bed, smoothing the sleeves flat, matching the shoulders, exactly the way his grandmother had shown him with the first towel.

He held the shirt up to the light. Bright white, every fold crisp. He set it on top of the stack and shouted down the hall, "Same time next week?"

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A desert is often defined as a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters, or 10 inches, of rain a year.
story:
Kate had never expected a camping trip to involve graphs, but there she sat on a flat rock by the campsite, tracing her finger over a wrinkled worksheet while Priya boiled water on the camp stove. The assignment from Ms. De Vries was due the day they got back: compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs. Kate had assumed she could sketch something from memory and be done with it. Now, staring at the rainfall bars for the Atacama Desert, she wasn't so sure.

"Look at this," she said, holding the page out to Priya. "Some months here show almost nothing. Like, two millimeters. Some show zero."

Priya leaned over, steam curling past her face. "Zero? How is anything alive there?"

That was the question, and it nagged at Kate all afternoon while they gathered firewood. The two of them had chosen this project over the volcano poster because Mustafa had advocated for it, saying the graphs were more interesting than pictures of lava. Kate had gone along. She was starting to wonder if that had been a mistake, or if the mistake was hers alone for not actually looking at the data before they left.

When Mustafa came back from filling water jugs, he dropped onto the log beside her and peered at the worksheet. "What's the rainforest graph look like?"

She flipped the page over. The bars there towered over the desert's, month after month, some of them taller than three hundred millimeters. Side by side, the graphs looked like two different planets. "The rainforest gets more rain in some single months than the desert gets in years," she said slowly, doing the arithmetic twice on the corner of the page.

Mustafa frowned. "So how little does the desert get total? Is there a cutoff, or is it just 'pretty dry'?"

Kate dug through her pack for the field guide Ms. De Vries had lent them, its cover already damp from the tent. She found the climate chapter, ran her finger down the margin, and stopped. She read the line twice. "It says a desert is a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters of rain a year. Ten inches."

Mustafa sat up straighter. "Wait. Ten inches? It snows way more than that back home in a winter."

Kate did the conversion in her notebook, and the pencil nearly stopped in her hand. Their own town, the place with slush and gray skies and snow days, got more precipitation than that. But somewhere in her memory was a documentary about Antarctica, ice everywhere, and she recalled the narrator calling it a desert. She had thought that was a mistake in the show, or maybe a joke. Now she wasn't sure.

"Let's test it," she said, and pulled the atlas from the supply bin. She found a precipitation map, found the regions with the lowest shading, and set the field guide's definition beside it. The polar regions matched the driest colors. "A cold, snowy place can count as a desert," she said. "By the rainfall, not the temperature."

Priya came over from the stove and studied the map with her arms crossed. "So when I wrote 'deserts are hot' in my notes last year, was I just biased because I only ever saw pictures of sand?"

"Maybe," Kate said. "Or maybe the pictures were all we were shown."

They sat with that for a while, the fire popping as the light went orange behind the trees. Kate taped both graphs into her notebook side by side and wrote the definition across the top in careful letters. Mustafa suggested they ask Ms. De Vries whether they could add the polar example to their presentation, and Priya said they should argue for it, even if it wasn't required.

Kate looked at the little column of numbers she had added for the Atacama, then at the towering rainforest bars, and underlined one figure twice.

"Two hundred and forty-one millimeters," she said. "Not quite under the line. Let's check the other one."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept up high and out of reach, because young children explore by putting things in their mouths.
story:
Leo had agreed to babysit for exactly one reason, which was that Ms. Georgiou across the street paid twenty dollars and had a television bigger than his. She left him with a toddler named after her grandmother, a list of emergency numbers, and the sentence, "She puts everything in her mouth, so watch her."

For the first ten minutes this seemed like an exaggeration. The child chewed on a rubber giraffe, a coaster, and the corner of a board book about a lion, which Leo read aloud twice because the child seemed to believe the lion was a personal friend. "He's a carnivore," Leo said, pointing at the illustration. "That means he eats meat, not babysitters." The child applauded this, possibly for the wrong reasons.

Then Leo got up to find the kitchen and the promised snacks, and on his way back through the living room he stopped. On the low coffee table sat a dispenser of children's vitamins, bright orange, gummy, and shaped like small bears. The child was on the far side of the rug, banging the coaster against the floor. Leo did the math slowly, the way he did word problems. Low table, small gummy bears, a person whose entire life philosophy was putting things in her mouth.

He picked up the vitamins and held them while he thought. He was not sure this was even his business. But Ms. Georgiou had been diligent about the emergency numbers, three of them, taped to the fridge, which suggested she worried in an organized way. And the vitamins were orange and sweet and, to a toddler, indistinguishable from candy. He carried them to the kitchen and set them on the highest shelf, above the microwave, where he himself needed a chair to reach. Then he did a slow circuit of the living room, checking under the table and behind the couch. He found a bottle of glass cleaner under the end table and exiled that to the shelf as well.

When he returned, the child had reached the coffee table and was patting the empty spot where the vitamins had been, with the expression of someone whose restaurant had lost its reservation. "They've moved," Leo told her. "Up high. Out of reach. That's where medicines and cleaning products live now, because you explore with your mouth, and that is a problem." She stared at him, then chewed on the table leg instead.

When Ms. Georgiou came home she found the vitamins on the high shelf, and she stood in the kitchen doorway holding her keys. "You moved these?"

"They were on the coffee table," Leo said, deciding not to clarify whose fault that was.

She looked at the shelf, then at the child, who was now gnawing the rubber giraffe with new determination. "Twenty-five dollars," Ms. Georgiou said. "And next time you get the good snacks."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973.
story:
The phone sat heavy in Theo's pocket, heavier than it had any right to be, like it knew it was the first thing he had ever really owned. He climbed onto the bus after track practice and slid into the seat next to Ayat, who took one look at his face and grinned.

"You got it. You actually got it." Ayat held out a hand. "Let me see this historical artifact."

Theo passed it over carefully, the way you'd hand someone an egg. Last Saturday at the phone store, while his mom filled out forms, he had asked the cashier how long people had been walking around with phones in their pockets, expecting some big number, decades and decades. The cashier had laughed and said the first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973. Theo had been skeptical, because that was only about fifty years ago, which felt impossible, but he had checked it on the store's display model anyway. It was true.

"So it works?" Maika called from the seat behind them, leaning over. "Did you call anyone yet?"

"My grandma," Theo admitted. "For two minutes. I panicked and said I had to go."

The bus jolted over the rail crossing and the phone slipped from Ayat's hands, bounced off the metal edge of the seat, and clattered into the aisle. Theo's stomach dropped the whole way down with it. Ayat scooped it up, but the screen had a thin white line running across it, bright and crooked, like a crack in ice.

"I'm so sorry," Ayat said. "I'll pay for it. Whatever it costs."

Theo stared at the line. His mom had said one rule above all others: take care of it, because there would not be another. His first instinct was to shove the phone in his bag, insulate it in a sock, and pretend the crack wasn't there until it somehow disappeared. But he had been thinking, all morning, about a paradox his science teacher kept mentioning: hiding a problem never makes it smaller, it only makes it harder to see. He didn't entirely believe that yet.

He turned the phone over in his hands, tilted it toward the window light, then pressed the power button and held his breath. The screen lit up. He swiped, opened the camera, took a photo of Maika's startled face. Everything worked. The line was just a line.

"It still works," Theo said slowly. "But I'm going to tell my mom tonight. Before she finds it herself." He looked at Ayat, whose shoulders had come down an inch. "And you're coming with me. You can tell her the part about the bus."

"Deal," Ayat said.

Maika leaned between them. "Can I text it to my phone so I have proof Ayat broke something famous?"

Theo laughed and typed his first text ever, with one thumb, very slowly: look what you did.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 33 of the Canadian Charter, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and the override can be renewed.
story:
Dominic had spread his Charter of Rights study sheet across his grandfather's kitchen table, right beside a plate of biscuits, when the TV news said the words "notwithstanding clause" and both his grandfather and his aunt started talking at once.

"See?" his aunt said, pointing her biscuit at the screen. "They can just take your rights away."

"That is not what it means," his grandfather said.

Dominic slid his sheet closer to the TV as if it could absorb the argument. He had a presentation for Ms. Han on Monday, and he was supposed to explain one right in his own words, and instead the whole family was fighting about Section 33.

"They could use it on you," his aunt went on. "Five years, gone. Then what?"

"Then five more," his grandfather said, "if they renew it. It is not a forever thing, it is a five year thing."

Dominic found the section on his sheet and ran his finger down it. "Wait. So Parliament, or a provincial legislature, can override certain rights, but only for up to five years. And then the override can be renewed." He looked up. "That's like a library book. You borrow it, you can renew it, but the book still exists."

"Terrible analogy," said his cousin from the doorway, but she was grinning.

"It's a great analogy." Dominic tested it out loud, the way he'd test a fire alarm. "So the rights don't disappear. Somebody just decides not to follow them for a while. Five years at a time." He chewed a biscuit. "That's actually weirder than taking them away. It's like saying, I know the rule, and I'm breaking it on purpose, with paperwork."

His grandfather laughed so hard he had to put down his tea.

Dominic's cousin picked up the study sheet. "What if you forgot to renew it, though? Like when you had that library book and felt guilt for three weeks?"

"That was you," Dominic said. "And you left it in the flammable bin next to the fireplace, which is not the library's return slot."

"That bin said recycling."

"It said flammable materials, and you threw a book in it."

His aunt was still frowning at the muted TV. "But they could prolong it forever. Five years, five years, five years."

"That's why you vote," his grandfather said, tapping the table, "so the people doing the overriding have to face you eventually."

Dominic wrote at the bottom of his sheet: think library book. Then he looked up.

"Grandpa, can I practise my presentation on you? You play Ms. Han."

"I will play the hardest Ms. Han who ever lived," his grandfather said, and cleared his throat. "Begin."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
story:
The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Cole's heart was pounding so hard he could feel it in his ears. That was the whole reason he was here. Two weeks ago, standing up to give a history presentation, his heart had started racing and his breathing had gone quick and shallow, like his body believed something terrible was about to happen even though the only danger in the room was Aveer whispering "you're turning purple." Cole had been pessimistic about it ever since, convinced something was wrong with his heart, and his mom had finally booked this appointment.

"Cole," the nurse called, and he followed her down the hall.

The doctor listened to his chest, asked questions, and tapped something into a computer. "Your heart is perfectly healthy," she said. "What you're describing sounds like anxiety. Your body's fight-or-flight response. The adrenal glands release adrenaline, and adrenaline makes your heart beat faster and breathing speed up."

"So it's... stress?" Cole asked. "From a presentation?"

"Exactly. Your brain treats a room full of classmates a bit like a threat, even when nothing dangerous is actually happening."

Cole sat with that. He tried to devise a test for it, because it seemed strange that a body could be so wrong about danger. If the pounding only showed up before presentations and not during, say, gym class, then the trigger really was the presentation and not his heart itself. He thought back: the science fair, the tryout for the basketball team, the day he'd asked Malaika if she wanted to study together. Pounding, pounding, pounding. Dodgeball on Friday, nothing at all.

"Here's the thing," the doctor said, handing him a printout. "There are coping strategies. Slow breathing, practiced beforehand. And it helps to set some boundaries, like not taking on five presentations in one week just to prove something."

Cole remembered the science fair. He'd volunteered for it alone, in front of everyone, mostly because Mr. Farah had said it would look good on scholarship applications someday. At the time it had felt brave. Now he wondered if it had just been a bad trade, trading three nights of sleep for a line on an application. He still couldn't decide.

On the way out, he passed the scale in the hallway and stopped. His heart was hammering again, badly, worse than before the presentation. He checked his watch and counted. Fastest yet.

The only dangerous thing in the room was the blood pressure cuff he was about to dodge.

"Do I have to get that too?" he asked the nurse.

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: Some Spanish verbs change their stem in the future tense: "tener" (to have) becomes "tendré," meaning "I will have," not "teneré."
story:
Ella sat at the kitchen table with her Spanish paragraph spread in front of her. Mr. Tremblay had circled one word in red ink and written "See me" beside it. The paragraph was about her plans for next year, and the circled word was "teneré" in the sentence "El año que viene teneré un perro."

She had written it the way she wrote every other future tense verb. "Hablar" became "hablaré," "visitar" became "visitaré," so "tener" should become "teneré." But the red circle said otherwise. Her mom set a glass of milk on the table and asked what was wrong. "Mr. Tremblay circled one verb," Ella said, "and I can't figure out why. Everything else is fine."

She pulled out her phone and texted Zara, who was in the other Spanish class. "Did you get anything circled on the plans paragraph?" Zara wrote back a minute later: "Yes! My 'poder' came back circled too." Ella frowned at the screen. "Poder" should become "poderé," the same way everything else worked. Two circled verbs, both wrong, and the pattern, whatever it was, hid somewhere she couldn't see it directly.

She got out a fresh sheet of paper and made a chart. Down the left side she listed regular verbs like "hablar" and "comer," and down the right side she listed "tener," "poder," "venir," and "salir." Then she opened her textbook to the future tense chapter and hunted for sentences. "Saldré mañana," one exercise said. "Vendrán en junio," said another. The regular verbs kept their stems whole, but the ones in her right-hand column all lost something. "Tener" didn't become "teneré" at all. It became "tendré."

She texted Alejandro, who had spent a summer in Mexico with his cousins. He replied fast. "It's tendré, not teneré. Tener becomes tendré, it means I will have." Ella wrote it at the top of her chart. The stem changed and the e turned up in the ending. She fixed her sentence: "El año que viene tendré un perro." Then she added two more sentences to the paragraph for good measure, one about how she would donate her old bike to the shelter, and one about how she and the dog would be agile enough by spring to join the weekend agility class at the park.

The next morning she handed the corrected paragraph to Mr. Tremblay before the bell. He read it, looked up, and pulled a red pen from his pocket. "One more thing," he said. "You wrote that you'll feed the dog like a scavenger. Vulture, Ella." Ella took the paper back and crossed out "buitre," laughing. "Fine. Next year I'll feed him dog food."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Wool shrinks in hot, sloshing water because tiny scales on each wool fibre open up and lock onto neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter. This is called felting.
story:
Jordan stood in the middle of Grandpa's garage, which now held a washer and dryer instead of the old woodworking bench, staring at three garbage bags of laundry his mom had left there with one instruction: "Figure it out before Sunday." He was supposed to be learning to do a whole load from start to finish, and he'd promised Malaika he could handle it, but the bags held everything mixed together: towels, jeans, T-shirts, and, folded in paper at the bottom of the second bag, Grandpa's hand-knitted cream sweater with a note that said, "Wash gently, please."

His first move was to classify the pile into heaps on the garage floor: darks, lights, whites, and a fourth heap he wasn't sure about, which held the sweater and a woolly pair of socks. He texted Malaika a photo of the heaps, and she wrote back, "The mystery pile is wool, obviously. Wash it cold or don't wash it." Loukas, who came over to help in exchange for snacks, shrugged and said everything could just go in on hot, because hot water got things cleaner.

They compromised on science. Jordan had a theory that whatever made wool different had to be invisible, something about the yarn itself, and that hot water might be the trigger. To test it, he took one of the woolly socks and ran it under the hottest tap water in the garage sink, sloshing it around in a bucket for a few minutes while Loukas timed him. The sock came out noticeably smaller, tight and dense where it had been stretchy, almost like felt. The other sock, swished in cold water, stayed exactly the same size. "So it's the hot water plus the sloshing," Jordan said, laying the two socks side by side. "Something in the wool reacts."

Malaika arrived just then with her phone, and after a search she held it up. "It's called felting," she said. "Tiny scales on each wool fibre open up in hot, sloshing water and lock onto the neighbouring fibres, and that pulls the knit tighter." Jordan looked at his shrunken sock, which now would barely fit a doll, and felt both sick and relieved. Sick because he'd ruined a sock, relieved because the sweater was still sitting clean and dry in its paper, and because the pattern was clear. Wool meant cold water and no sloshing, and now he knew why the note said "gently."

The rest of the day went better than the start. He ran the darks and towels on hot, the lights on warm, and washed the sweater alone in cold water, squeezing it gently instead of wringing it, the way you'd handle something porous that could soak through and change. When everything came out of the dryer, he and Loukas folded it into a lopsided but real stack on the workbench, and Jordan laid the two socks on top like evidence. He took a photo of the whole load, folded sweater included, and sent it to his mom with the words, "Sunday is handled."

Then he dropped the little shrunken sock into his pocket, deciding he'd keep it as a prototype for a keychain or just as proof of what he'd figured out, and switched off the garage light.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
Mya slid two photocopies across the dinner table, one in each hand, like she was dealing cards. "Dad, you're the British soldier. Mom, you're the colonial militiaman. Vada, read the time out loud."

Vada, still holding her fork, raised an eyebrow. "This is why you invited me to dinner?"

"Just read it."

Vada cleared her throat. "April morning, 1775, Lexington. Both witnesses say the same thing happened at the same spot. Both say the other side fired first."

"Right." Mya tapped the left page. "The British witness says a colonist hiding behind a wall fired first. The colonial witness says a British soldier fired first. Historians still don't know who actually fired that shot. Nobody does. Not after two hundred and fifty years." She looked around the table. "So here's my test. Dad, Mom, read your accounts out loud, but don't say which side is yours."

Her dad frowned but read. Her mom followed. Same green, same smoke, same crack of muskets in the pale light. Then they argued, gently, about who sounded like the villain of their page.

Mya leaned forward. "Which one is the British account?"

Her dad pointed to the right page. Her mom pointed to the left. Vada pointed at both and then pulled her hand back.

"You can't tell," Mya said. "That's the point. Each account is robust on its own. It has details, it sounds honest. It's only when you put them side by side that they contradict." She had spent three days on this, ever since Mr. Tran had handed the history club the two accounts and said only, "Notice whatever you notice." She'd assumed the answer would pop out. It hadn't. So tonight she'd built a test around a simple principle: if you strip away the labels, a fair reader still can't pick the truth.

Vada set down her fork, which she had been loading with rice the whole time. "Wait. This matters for my thing. For my essay." She pulled a crumpled assignment sheet from her pocket and smoothed it on the tablecloth. "I have to write about a fight on the bus last week. I was going to write what I saw. But Tanya told me the eighth graders started it, and she was sitting closer than me."

"So who started it?" Mya's dad asked.

"I don't know," Vada said slowly, like the words surprised her. "I was going to say the eighth graders, because that's what everyone says. But I only actually saw the middle of it." She looked at the photocopied pages, then at Mya. "Can I borrow these? I want to interview two people from the bus before I write anything."

Mya pushed both pages across. "Verify everything."

Her mom laughed and started stacking plates. Vada was already writing questions on the back of her napkin, and outside the window a streetlamp buzzed on.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
story:
Rosalie kept a small blue notebook under her mattress, and tonight she wrote in it with a flashlight: "Day 41. Nothing yet." Her older cousin had gotten her first period at ten, which had seemed ancient history until Rosalie turned twelve in March and started counting. The notebook was her way of testing a theory, though she hadn't called it that yet.

At Kenzo's house on Saturday, she found Kenzo and Daniyal at the kitchen table with a bowl of popcorn between them. Kenzo's older sister was on the phone in the hallway, laughing about something with her friend. Rosalie caught the words "my period" and looked away, feeling like she'd read someone's mail.

"My sister got hers at fourteen," Kenzo said, once the sister had wandered upstairs. "She was the last of her friends. She used to keep a calendar with little stars on it, like she was waiting for a bus that was always late."

"My sister got hers at ten," Rosalie said. "Ten."

Daniyal shrugged. "My mom's a nurse. She says there's this big CDC survey, like huge, thousands of girls, and the middle age, the median, is about twelve. But she said the normal range around it is really wide, so basically anytime is normal-normal." He ate a fistful of popcorn. "Which, if you think about it, means nobody can predict anything, which is the most annoying kind of fact."

Rosalie turned that over all the way home. A median of about twelve meant half the girls in her grade were probably before her and half after, and a wide range meant even ten and fourteen both fit inside normal. So her cousin being early told her nothing about herself, and neither did the notebook's forty-one empty days. The data was one thing she couldn't see directly, but she could test her own small piece of it. That night she made a treaty with herself: stop counting days, keep three supplies in her backpack, and act like it was a bus that would come whenever it came. Sealing the treaty required chocolate, so she ate the last of the Easter candy concealed behind the vegetable drawer, where her dad thought nobody looked.

On Monday she took the notebook out from under the mattress anyway. She didn't write a day number. Instead she wrote "wide range" and drew a crooked bus, then added a window with no driver in it, because the schedule was clearly not up to her. She slid the notebook into her backpack next to the supplies, zipped it shut, and went downstairs for breakfast.

Kenzo met her at the corner, agile as always, hopping the puddle from last night's rain. "Still waiting on the bus?" she asked.

"Stopped checking my watch," Rosalie said. "Want my fruit roll-up? I'm not hungry."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: The 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right.
story:
The bleachers in the gymnasium were folded against the wall, and the whole seventh grade sat on the floor in wobbly rows while Mr. Siddiqui set up the microphone at the free-throw line. James stood backstage with six other spellers, card number four pinned to his shirt, and watched Calla pace between the volleyball standards. She had beaten him in the classroom bee on the word "silhouette," and she had beaten him in the school bee last year on "camouflage." If she beat him today, it would be three years in a row, and that pattern felt like a rule he couldn't break.

Kingsley leaned against the stage curtain, chewing a straw. "You look like you're solving a math problem," he said.

"I am, sort of," James said. "Every time it comes down to me and Calla, she wins. I keep trying to figure out why."

"She reads more than you."

"That's not a reason, that's an insult." James pulled at his card. What he wanted wasn't just to win. He wanted to know whether the pattern was real or whether last year and the year before had been luck dressed up as destiny.

The bee began. A boy misspelled "legible," and a girl from second period went out on "gratitude." Mr. Siddiqui's voice rolled up into the rafters, calm as a radio announcer. When James stepped to the microphone, his first word was "retrieve," which meant to go and get something back, and he spelled it slowly, like he was carrying it a long way. Calla got "hereditary," as in a trait passed down through a family, and James thought, of course she did, like her winning was hereditary too.

By round nine it was only the two of them. Calla spelled "organism." James spelled "resilient." Round ten: she got "threshold," he got "vacant." Round eleven, round twelve. Mr. Siddiqui kept flipping to the last page of his word list, and James noticed something: the pronouncer's forehead was shiny, and the list was getting thin. The words weren't running out because the spellers were failing. They were running out because the spellers kept getting them right.

"I know what happens now," Kingsley whispered from the curtain, loud enough for James to hear. "In 2019 the Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. Eight of them. They just gave up and crowned everybody."

James felt something loosen in his chest. The pattern of Calla beating him wasn't a rule at all. It was just what had happened before, and what happened before could stop.

Round fourteen came. Calla spelled "turbulence" without a wobble. James stepped up and received "apparent," and spelled it with the double p and double r, and heard the bell stay silent.

Mr. Siddiqui looked at his final page, then at his watch, then out at the rows of seventh graders sitting cross-legged on the glossy floor. He cleared his throat. "Ladies and gentlemen," he said, "it appears we have two champions." He held up the nearly empty list like a referee holding up a card.

Calla turned to James and stuck out her hand. "Trophy's at the display case," she said. "I say we make them fit both our names on the little plaque."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.
story:
Adam stood in front of a glass case in the history museum, staring at a small leather book with cracked binding. Inside was the diary of a settler named E. Hobbs, written in faded brown ink in 1873. His worksheet asked him to use a primary source to explain why people moved west, and he had forty minutes before the bus left.

"You're on your third paragraph of nothing," said Jan, leaning over his shoulder. Marie-Soleil was already scribbling on her own sheet two cases away.

"I don't get what the diary is supposed to tell me," Adam said. "It just says they crossed a river and a wheel broke."

Mr. Shevchenko, the museum guide, passed by and said, "Read like a detective. What does the writer notice? What does he never mention?" Then he moved on to help another group.

Adam bent closer. Hobbs counted his oxen, described the grass, mentioned his wife's cough. Then, on the fourth page, a line jumped out: "If we hold the claim five years, the land is ours, all one hundred and sixty acres, and no landlord can take it back."

Adam froze. He had seen that number before. Last summer, in his grandfather's attic, he had opened a tin box while looking for badminton rackets and found a stiff paper document with a wax seal. His grandfather had held it up to the window and said, "This is how our family got the farm." The paper had said the same thing, 160 acres, five years. Adam had thought it was trivial at the time, just an old receipt. Now he wondered if it was the whole answer.

He tried a small test. If land was the reason people moved, then the diary should mention land more than anything else. He made tallies in his notebook, a way to classify each entry: weather, repairs, illness, land. Land won, nine mentions against three for everything else.

"Marie-Soleil," he whispered, "does your diary mention the Homestead Act?"

She scanned her pages. "Mine calls it the Act. Same thing?"

"Maybe." Adam read again. Hobbs wrote about "filing at the land office" and "proving up." It fit, like a vessel filling with water, every line finding its level around one central fact: people moved west because the United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.

He wrote his answer, then copied Hobbs's exact sentence as evidence, including the broken wheel, because that detail showed how badly they wanted the land and kept going anyway.

On the bus, Adam texted his grandfather a photo of his finished worksheet. The reply came before the museum was out of sight: "Come by Saturday. I'll show you where the fence corners met, all four of them."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: A word problem can be turned into an equation: if a taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometre and a ride costs 15, then 3 + 2k = 15, so k = 6.
story:
Parker slid his chair up to the table just as Mr. Martínez set a folded receipt in the middle of it. "Warm-up problem," Mr. Martínez said. "First team to crack it gets the window seats."

Anita grabbed the receipt before anyone else could. "This is my grandma's," she said. "From the taxi on Saturday. She thinks the driver overcharged her, and she wants proof." Her voice was tight. Anita did not like being wrong, and she liked losing even less.

Parker read over her shoulder. The paper showed a base charge of three dollars, then two dollars per kilometre, and a total of fifteen dollars at the bottom. Across the table, Jeremie was already scribbling guesses. "Five kilometres," he said. "Two times five is ten, plus three is thirteen. Close."

"Close is wrong," Anita said. She tried six. Two times six was twelve, and twelve plus three was fifteen. "It's six kilometres." She reached for Mr. Martínez's answer sheet, but Parker put his hand flat over it.

"Wait," he said. "You guessed it. Guessing won't work next time." He turned the receipt over and wrote in his most meticulous handwriting: 3 + 2k = 15. "My sister does this. You're allowed to take three off, but you have to take it off both sides, or the equals sign breaks." He drew a line down the middle of the equation. "It's like symmetry. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other."

Anita frowned at the line. "Both sides."

"Watch." He crossed out the three on the left, then crossed out a three on the right, turning fifteen into twelve. "Now it's just 2k equals twelve."

"So k is six," Jeremie said slowly. "Because two times six is twelve."

"Same answer," Anita admitted, "but his way doesn't depend on luck." She pulled the receipt back toward herself and checked the trip meter her grandmother had written on the back: 6 km. The numbers matched. Anita copied Parker's equation onto a fresh sheet, careful this time, and slid it into her folder. "I'm showing my grandmother tonight. She can take this to the company and ask for her money back if it doesn't match."

Mr. Martínez walked past, glanced at Parker's crossed-out threes, and gave a single nod. He did not disclose the answer on his sheet, but he did move two chairs to the window. "Window seats," he said. "Earned."

Parker sat down and looked at the equation still on the back of the receipt. Then he wrote a new one underneath, 3 + 2k = 21, just to see if the trick would hold twice.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In French, "Je voudrais..." means "I would like..." and sounds more polite than "Je veux...", which means "I want..."
story:
Grandma's kitchen smelled like onion soup, which Ivy decided was perfect, since tonight the whole house was going to become a restaurant in Paris. Grandma had printed a menu, taped it to the pantry door, and put on her reading glasses, which apparently turned her into a French waiter. Ivy had a plan, too: by Sunday she wanted to order lunch in French on her class trip, all by herself, without her notebook.

"Bonsoir," Grandma said in a dramatic voice, gliding over with an invisible notepad. "What will Madame have?"

Ivy had practiced on the bus and in the bathtub, so she went first with the words she knew best. "Je veux le poulet," she said. "Et... combien ça coûte?"

Grandma's eyebrows shot up. She put one hand on her hip like an insulted actor. "Madame!" she gasped. "Out of my restaurant! We do not serve people who talk like that!"

Ivy sat back, staring at the pantry menu. She hadn't dropped a plate or used a wrong number; her question about cost had even come out smoothly. So the problem had to be hiding in the first sentence, in the tiny word "veux." It was the only part she'd changed since yesterday, when Grandma had smiled and poured her pretend water. She tested the idea, swapping in the other phrase from her worksheet. "Je voudrais le poulet, s'il vous plaît. Combien ça coûte?"

Grandma's whole face softened. "Ah, magnifique. Right this way, Madame." She scribbled on the air with her invisible pen.

"Wait," Ivy said, laughing. "That's it? One little word?"

Rose, who was watching through a video call propped against the sugar bowl, shook her head. "My brother told me that. 'Je voudrais' means 'I would like,' and 'Je veux' means 'I want.' One sounds polite and one sounds like you're demanding chicken."

"Like the chicken owes you money," Grandma added, straightening her glasses. She went to the counter and picked up a small paper bag from the pharmacy, tucking her prescription inside it so it wouldn't get lost in the restaurant chaos. Then she returned, calm and official, as if no one had ever been thrown out of a Paris bistro in her kitchen.

They ran the scene again, Ivy ordering soup, bread, and even dessert, asking the price each time. Grandma transmitted each imaginary dish to the imaginary kitchen with a little bow. When Ivy ordered her made-up chocolate mousse, she leaned forward and asked, very politely, whether it came with two spoons.

"Deux cuillères," Grandma said, and slid an empty bowl toward her with both hands.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
story:
Zoe had cancelled three appointments since September, and today the receptionist had refused to let her reschedule again. So now she sat in the waiting room of Dr. Iyer's office, gripping a magazine about dinosaurs that she wasn't reading. Beside her, Tia flipped through the same issue and read aloud that sauropods were the largest herbivores ever to walk the earth, which seemed to Zoe like a strange thing for a doctor's office to care about.

"You're doing that thing with your thumb," Tia said. "The wringing thing."

"I'm fine," Zoe said, and her thumb kept going.

The problem was needles. In September the shot had seemed like a small, ordinary thing, and she'd skipped it anyway because it was easier. In October just walking through the door had felt worse. By November she'd made her mother call and cancel from the car, and today her heart was doing something vigorous against her ribs, like it was trying to leave before she did. She had begun to suspect the dates mattered. She pulled out the little appointment card and checked: the three cancelled dates corresponded exactly to the three times the fear had grown bigger. Every time she ran away, the next time was scarier. She was teaching herself something, and it wasn't the right thing.

"That's backwards," she said out loud.

"What is?"
