"I keep dodging it so I'll feel better, and I do, for like an hour. And then the next appointment is worse. It's like the dodging is the thing making it grow." She looked at the card. "I want to test it. Today I stay, and I look right at it. If I'm right, staying should make the next one easier."

Tia lowered the dinosaur magazine. "You're going to look at the needle? Voluntarily?"

"That's the experiment."

The nurse called her name before she could lose her nerve. In the exam room, Dr. Iyer was an older man with brisk, vigorous movements, snapping on gloves and swabbing Zoe's arm before she had finished sitting down. He asked about school, about sleep, about whether she worried a lot. She admitted she did, that her stomach dropped before every presentation, that she'd been skipping things. He said the words for it, anxiety and stress, the way he'd say asthma or a sprained ankle, and asked what she did to cope. "Not coming here," Zoe said, and told him her theory about the cancelled dates lined up with the fear getting worse each time.

"That lines up with what we see," Dr. Iyer said. He didn't make a speech about it. He just said, "Some things you can't outrun forever," and lifted the syringe.

Zoe kept her eyes open. She watched the whole thing, which lasted about four seconds and felt like a mosquito with better aim. Her body had braced for something enormous, and what arrived was small, and her body had no idea what to do with the mismatch.

"See?" Tia said in the hallway afterward, holding the door. "Nothing to it. I told you." Then Tia, who had given the speech about bravery, who had never skipped anything in her life, looked at Zoe's tiny bandaged arm, turned a spectacular grey colour, and sat straight down on the floor.

Zoe went to get the nurse, trying not to laugh, and heard herself say, "Don't worry. It only looks scary the first hundred times you look away."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869.
story:
Charles slid his stool closer to the lab bench, where Ms. Ramos had taped a photocopied periodic table beside the gas taps. The paper smelled faintly of toner, and the morning light caught the dust on the window fume hood. On the whiteboard she had written three questions, and the first one read: "How many protons does gold have?" Charles wanted the answer, because Ms. Ramos was keeping a leaderboard for the unit, and Kingston was already two points ahead of him.

He traced his finger along the rows of small boxes. Each box held a symbol, a name, and a number in the top corner, and at first the numbers looked random, like locker combinations. Then he noticed that gold's number, 79, matched a second smaller number printed below the symbol. He checked oxygen. Eight and eight. He checked carbon. Six and six. So the top number, the atomic number, was a key. If it told him the number of protons, he could find the protons for any element on the table without asking anyone.

He tested it in the margin of his notebook. Oxygen, eight protons. Iron, twenty-six. He was on neodymium when Kingston leaned over from the next bench. "You figured out the protons thing?" Kingston whispered. Charles nodded and covered his margin with his palm, because the rule felt like a treasure he wanted to keep for the quiz on Friday.

The room reminded him of the science museum his class had visited last fall. There had been a long timeline on the wall near the entrance, and Kaylie had stopped in front of an old chart with gaps in it, like a checkerboard missing squares. She had read the caption out loud. "Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869," she had said, and then she had counted the empty spaces with her finger. Charles remembered standing there thinking the table had always existed, complete, like a map of a country that was finished. Learning that it had once been smaller and unfinished had made the boxes on the classroom wall feel newer, almost fragile.

He went back to his sheet. Beside the modern table, Ms. Ramos had pinned a black-and-white copy of that old chart, its edges curling. Charles thought that Mendeleev must have reasoned the same way he just had, hunting for a pattern in numbers he could not see with his eyes, the way you could not see protons themselves, only the clues they left behind. In the corner of the lab, the red dot of the spectroscope laser blinked on and off as the student there adjusted her settings, and someone at the far bench laughed at a beaker that had turned an unexpected shade of green. Ms. Ramos had mentioned last week that some of the older equipment in the room, the wooden balance in the cabinet, was nearly obsolete, replaced by digital scales, though she still kept it because she liked it. Charles thought a table from 1869 was not like that. It had been modified over the years, boxes added, but the pattern underneath still worked, and the proof was right there in his margin, in his own careful rows of numbers.

He raised his hand for Ms. Ramos to check his answers, then lowered it again. Better to double-check one more element first, he decided, and he ran his finger along the bottom rows toward uranium.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: A testimonial uses a famous or admired person to endorse something, even though that person may have no special knowledge about it and may be paid.
story:
The group chat lit up at 9:04 on a Tuesday night, right when Quinn had promised herself she would hibernate under her blanket until morning.

Matis: HAVE YOU SEEN THE NEW FROSTLINE DUNKS. Trennon Blake wears them. THE Trennon Blake.
Maxwell: those are so sick
Matis: everyone on the travel team is getting them. literally everyone. you'll be the only one in old shoes.
Quinn typed back: How much?
Matis: 180
Quinn: one hundred eighty dollars because a basketball player wears them?

She set her phone down, then picked it up again. Matis had been saving allowance money since June for a new skateboard, and now every dollar was about to march off toward sneakers. Something about it bugged her, the way a wrong answer bugs you before you figure out why it's wrong.

Quinn: question. did Trennon Blake pick those shoes himself?
Matis: he obviously picked them, they're HIS signature
Maxwell: wait my cousin works at the sports store. she says the company designs them and pays him to wear them
Matis: paid?? source??
Maxwell: she showed me a magazine ad once. it says "Trennon Blake" in tiny letters at the bottom but under that it says he's paid to be in it
Quinn: so it's a testimonial. a famous person endorsing something, even if they don't actually know anything special about it, and they might be getting paid.
Matis: he's a BASKETBALL PLAYER. he knows shoes.
Quinn: does he know shoemaking? or just running around in them like everybody else?

There was a long pause, three dots appearing and vanishing. Quinn decided to run a test, the way Mr. Lombardi had them test ideas in science. She sent a screenshot of the shoe ad next to a screenshot of another ad, one where a famous singer held a brand of motor oil.

Quinn: would you buy motor oil because she says so?
Matis: no that's dumb, she's a singer
Quinn: so why shoes because he says so?
Maxwell: yo

The chat went quiet again. Quinn chewed her thumbnail. She hadn't meant to embarrass Matis in front of Maxwell, and for a second she worried she had. Then she sent one more message, careful this time.

Quinn: I'm not saying they're bad shoes. I'm saying "everyone has them" isn't a reason, and "Trennon Blake wears them" isn't either. we could look up actual reviews. like, systematic. read twenty of them and count how many mention the heel falling apart.
Matis: ...fine. do it at lunch.

At lunch the next day, Matis slid his tray down next to hers with the dignity of someone who had lost an argument but refused to admit it out loud. "Seventeen out of twenty," he muttered, pulling out his phone. "Seventeen reviews say the heel wears out in three months."

"Maxwell's cousin says the old model lasted a year," Quinn said, "for half the price."

Matis stared at the screen for a long moment. Then he opened his banking app, the one where his skateboard fund lived, and looked at the number for a while.

"Okay," he said. "New plan." He tapped the screen twice, like casting a ballot in an election only he could vote in. "Skateboard first. Shoes when these ones actually fall apart." He paused, then grinned. "And when they do, I'm getting whatever brand Maxwell's cousin says lasts longest, not whatever Trennon Blake gets paid to jump in."

Quinn raised her chocolate milk. "To evidence."

"To evidence," Matis said, and clinked his juice box against it.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.
story:
The church smelled of pine polish and lilies, and the wooden pew creaked every time Taylor shifted her weight. On the folding table near the front sat a photograph of Grandma June holding a garden trowel, her hat crooked as always. Taylor's mother had asked her last night, quietly, if she would say a few words at the service, and Taylor had said yes before she could think too hard about it. Now the program in her hands felt like a live thing.

At the top of the program, in sparse gold lettering, was the word eulogy. She turned the paper over, turned it back, and stared at it. Kassidy slid into the pew beside her, tugging her skirt straight. "You still don't have one?" Kassidy whispered. "A memory. You said you'd pick one by this morning."

"I had nine this morning," Taylor whispered back. "Now I have none. They're all too small. She taught me to whistle through grass. That's not a speech." Her throat tightened, and she told herself the prickle behind her eyes was just a hormone thing, the way Kadence's older sister was always saying, crying over nothing, and she blinked hard until the front of the church came back into focus.

After the first hymn, Ms. Romano, who had been Grandma June's neighbor for twenty years, walked to the lectern. "I learned something from June years ago," she said. "She was the only person on our street who knew where words came from. She told me a eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died, and the word comes from Greek roots meaning to speak well of." She smiled down at Taylor for a second, then went on, but Taylor had stopped hearing the rest.

Speak well of. That was it, she realized. Not a list of accomplishments, not the biggest moment. The rule hiding inside the word itself. Her grandmother collected words the way some people acquired teacups, dusting them off, showing them to anybody who stood still long enough. Taylor suddenly knew which memory to pick, and she knew how to test it. She leaned toward Kassidy. "When I go up there, listen for whether I'm praising her or just listing stuff. If I'm listing, kick the pew."

"You're going up there?" Kassidy's voice cracked. "You have to tell Kadence, she's been dying to hear what you picked." Two rows ahead, Kadence twisted around, and Taylor held up the program and pointed at the word eulogy. Kadence frowned, then shrugged. Kassidy cupped her hands around her mouth. "Greek," she whispered loudly. "It means speak well of."

Kadence nodded slowly, like a puzzle piece had dropped into place for her too.

When Ms. Romano finished, the pastor called Taylor's name. Her knees felt borrowed, but she walked up anyway, and the lectern smelled like lemon cleaner and old varnish. "My grandma taught me words," she said, and her voice wobbled, then steadied. "She said whistling through a blade of grass was a lost art, and she made me practice until I got it, and when I finally did, she said, well of me. She said it exactly like that, like it was an old phrase. So here's the grass, and here's the whistle." She pulled a fat blade from her pocket, set it between her thumbs, and blew until a thin, reedy note floated up into the rafters, where the pine smell and the dust motes hung together in the light.

From the third pew, Kassidy kicked the wood once, softly, and Kadence was laughing and crying at the same time. Taylor folded the grass blade back into her pocket and said, "That one's for you, Grandma."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
Mila pulled a sweater the exact green-gray of lichen off the rack and held it up, but she wasn't really seeing it. In her head she was already in the gym next Friday, under the paper streamers, with everyone watching her stand stiff as a fence post while the music played. She could not dance. That was the whole problem, and no amount of shopping was going to fix it.

"Try the blue one," said Kierra, who was holding three dresses over one arm like she was on a mission. "Blue is authentic. It looks like it came from your grandmother's closet on purpose."

Antony, who had been dragged along and kept drifting toward the shoe section, held up his phone. "Okay, you two have to see this before you decide anything." He turned the screen toward them. On it, a white cockatoo with a yellow crest was bobbing its head and lifting its feet, clearly dancing. "His name's Snowball," Antony said. "He's a sulphur-crested cockatoo. In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed he could move in time to music. And when they sped the song up or slowed it down, he adjusted. He matched the new tempo."

Mila leaned closer. The bird wasn't just twitching. It was stepping left, right, swaying, landing on the beat. "Wait. Really? A bird?"

Kierra lowered the dresses. "If a bird can keep the beat, Mila, you can keep the beat."

Mila thought about that. Snowball couldn't read a dance manual. Nobody taught him steps. He heard the music and moved with it, and when the tempo changed, he changed too. Maybe keeping the beat was the actual secret, and everything else was decoration. There was only one way to find out. "Antony," she said, "play a song. Any song."

He started something fast, and Mila stood there in the aisle between the racks, shifting her weight side to side, counting the pulse under the music. One-two, one-two. When Antony secretly thumbed the speed control and slowed the song down, her swaying slowed with it, and when he cranked it up again, she caught back up, laughing now, half a step behind and then locked on.

"Ha!" Antony said. "It worked. You adjusted, like Snowball."

"It worked," Mila agreed, still moving. The stiff fence post in her imagination had turned into a person who could find a rhythm and hold it.

At the register, Kierra and Mila disagreed over which dress to buy, and Mila's mom, who had been waiting by the mirrors, mediated by suggesting they flip a coin. Kierra won the coin toss, but then she studied the blue dress again and changed her mind. "Actually, get the one you picked. You were the one dancing in it." Antony, who had sworn he would never go to the dance, tapped his phone and said, "Save me a song. Something with a tempo I can adjust to."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
story:
Levi slouched in front of the computer, clicking through a website his science teacher had assigned. The banner at the top said "MiracleGroMax: Doubles Your Tomato Yield, Guaranteed!" Below it, a farmer held an enormous tomato in both hands like a trophy. Levi leaned closer. He had a science project due Friday about claims and evidence, and this ad seemed too good to be true.

He scrolled down and found a testimonial from a man in Ohio who said he'd used the fertilizer and grown the biggest tomatoes of his life. "See, it works," Levi muttered, then stopped himself. One man's story wasn't the same as a tested claim. He remembered the unit on agriculture from class, the part about ancient farmers who saved seeds from their best plants, and how scientists later figured out which fertilizers actually helped by running careful trials. One farmer's lucky season could be good weather, rich soil, or plain luck.

He opened a chat window and typed, "Kassandra, you awake?"

"Barely," she wrote back. "What?"

"MiracleGroMax. The ad shows one farmer. How would they actually know it works?"

"Test it?" she suggested.

Levi thought about that. He imagined two identical pots of tomato seedlings on his windowsill. If he gave one pot the fertilizer and the other pot nothing, that would be a mess, because the fertilized pot might also get more sunlight by accident, or better soil. Then it hit him: the pot without the fertilizer had to get everything else exactly the same. Same soil, same water, same spot on the sill. He typed quickly, describing both pots, and added, "The one without fertilizer is called a control group."

"Like in class," Kassandra wrote. "Mr. Kovalenko would be proud."

Blaine joined the chat a minute later. "Just spray it on everything and see if stuff grows," he typed, which made Levi grin. He explained why that wouldn't tell you anything, because without a control you couldn't link the growth to the fertilizer itself. Any difference between the two groups had to come from that one thing, the fertilizer, if everything else stayed identical. Blaine sent back a thumbs up and, "Okay, I get it. Buy two pots."

The next morning Levi placed the pots side by side, labeled A and B, and measured each seedling with a ruler. "Thirty days," he told them. "Then we'll know." He watered both with the same small cup, set the fertilizer packet beside pot A, and took a photo to transmit to Mr. Kovalenko for approval. His phone buzzed with Kassandra's reply to the morning's picture before he even sat down: "My mom just bought the same fertilizer for her whole garden. All of it."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982.
story:
The poster outside Mr. García's classroom showed the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and the afternoon sun through the hallway window refracted off its plastic covering, scattering small bright patches across the words. Alexa stopped to read it for the third time that week, because on Friday every student had to stand up and explain one Charter right in their own words, and she still did not have hers.

"Still hunting?" Adnan asked, coming down the hall with his debate binder under his arm. He already knew his: the right to a lawyer, which he planned to deliver like a courtroom speech, since the debate team had a tournament next month and he wanted the practice.

"It's not the explaining that's stuck," Alexa said. She tapped the bottom corner of the poster, where a date sat in small print. "April 17, 1982. That's when the Charter became part of Canada's Constitution." She frowned at it. "Before that, what did people have? Nothing? Something else?"

"You could just pick section seven and be done," Adnan said. "Everyone does section seven. It's the conventional choice."

"That's why I don't want it." She copied the date into her notebook and stared at it while the light shifted on the glass. Her idea was simple: if the Charter had a birthday, then something must have existed before the birthday, the way a house exists before the renovation. She wanted to test it.

In the library she found a thick blue book on government, and Adnan found her there twenty minutes later, hunched over the index. "You were right to wonder," she said. "Before 1982 it wasn't that people had no rights at all. But the Charter, this exact list, only came in when it was proclaimed that day in April." She turned the book so he could see the printed date. "So when I explain my right, I can say it's written down in the Constitution, and that's been true since 1982. Before that, the same words didn't exist anywhere."

Adnan slid into the chair across from her. "Fine, but which right?"

Alexa pointed to the section on life, liberty and security of person, and under it the line about a fair hearing within a reasonable time. "This one. In my own words: the government can't just decide things about you in the dark. If it comes after you, you get to see the case, face your adversary, and answer back."

"That's yours," Adnan admitted. "I'm keeping the lawyer one."

On Friday, when her turn came, Alexa stood in front of the poster, the sunlight still moving across the plastic, and said the date first: "April 17, 1982, the day the Charter became part of the Constitution."

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean, so warm air rises over the land and moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it.
story:
Hannah slumped into a chair at the public library and spread her materials across the table: three books about South Asia, a printed article, and a note from Mr. Vargas that said, in red ink, "Your explanation of the monsoon is still wrong. Presentation Thursday. Try again."

The problem was that nobody in her sources came out and said why the rain arrived. They all agreed it did. One book had a picture of farmers wading through flooded rice paddies, and one had a diagram with big curved arrows, but the arrows just floated there like decorations. Kendrick dropped into the chair across from her and stole a grape from her snack bag.

"Still fighting the weather?" he asked.

"It fights back," Hannah said. "Mr. Vargas prohibited us from just reading our slides out loud, so I actually have to understand this thing." She pushed the diagram toward him. "Look. The arrows point from the ocean toward the land. In summer. Why would air do that?"

Kendrick squinted. "Air has somewhere better to be?"

Hannah laughed, then stopped laughing, because that was actually a thought. She flipped to the section on land and sea and read it twice. "Okay," she said slowly. "In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean." She put one hand flat on the table, like the land, and curved the other over her water bottle, like the sea. "So the land gets hot, hot air rises over the land, and then moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it." She dragged her curved hand toward her flat one. "That's the arrow. The ocean air is wet. It comes in, and it rains."

"That's it?" Kendrick said.

"That has to be it. It explains why the rain arrives right when the heat is worst. My cousin in India always complains about exactly that." She checked the clock above the reference desk and winced. The library closed in forty minutes, and her rough draft was one wrong sentence away from nothing. Brady arrived, out of breath, with a bag of rice from the school supplies box for their model, and for ten minutes they poured and swept and poured again while Hannah talked through her hands, summer after summer, ocean air flowing in and falling as rain onto the rice.

On the walk home, Hannah held her notes against the wind. "It matters," she said. "The rice needs that flood. Farmers plan everything around it." She grinned. "Kendrick, you fixed my whole presentation with one dumb joke."

"It's a gift," he said, and held the door.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.
story:
Nicholas had never done his own laundry before, and he was determined to get it right. His mother was home sick with a fever, and the basket in the hallway had grown into a small mountain, so he carried it three blocks to Mr. Hussain's laundromat with a list in his pocket: sort, wash, dry, fold. His friend Romane came along because her own wash was backed up too, and because she wanted the good dryer, the one near the window that she claimed ran hotter than the rest.

First came sorting. Nicholas spread the clothes across two plastic tables and tried to distinguish the darks from the lights, which was easy until he reached a grey towel that seemed to belong to both piles. Romane leaned over, plucked a red sock from his whites pile, and waved it like evidence. "This turns everything pink," she said. "Trust me. My whole soccer uniform is rose coloured now." He moved the sock, then checked a shirt pocket and found a crumpled receipt and one dime, which he pocketed with a small sense of victory.

While the first load sloshed, Nicholas scrubbed a table where somebody had spilled something sticky. Under the sink he found two spray bottles, one marked chlorine bleach and the other marked glass cleaner with ammonia. He was about to pour a splash of bleach into the cleaner bottle to make one super cleaner when Mr. Hussain hurried over from the counter. "Stop," he said, holding up both hands. "Never mix those two."

Nicholas read the labels again, frowning. "Why not?" he asked, because the warning on the back only said do not mix with ammonia-containing products, which told him nothing.

Romane pulled out her phone, typed for a moment, and held up the screen. "It says here chlorine bleach mixed with ammonia-containing cleaners releases chloramine, and it's a toxic gas." She looked from one bottle to the other. "So if you'd poured them together, we'd all be coughing out on the sidewalk." Nicholas set the bleach down slowly, the way he might set down something with teeth. He had been about to mix two ordinary cleaning bottles, the kind of thing that looked harmless, and the danger had been completely invisible until the words on the labels connected.

Right then the lights flickered and died, and the washing machines shuddered into silence. Mr. Hussain groaned, then disappeared through a back door, and a moment later a generator roared to life somewhere behind the wall. The machines woke up one by one, drumming again, and the laundromat filled with warm humid air that smelled of soap. Romane got her dryer by the window after all, and she did a little diagonal dance across the tiles in celebration.

When everything was dry, Nicholas folded his mother's shirts the way she liked, sleeves crossed over, then folded in half, and stacked them so the edges lined up straight. He kept back her softest blanket and a clean pillowcase for her fever, and on the way home he stopped at the corner store for lemon tea. Romane carried the basket up the stairs for him, and he pushed open the apartment door with his shoulder. "Mom," he called, "your laundry's done, and I brought tea."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Noah Webster's 1828 'American Dictionary of the English Language' promoted simpler spellings such as 'color' instead of 'colour', which became standard in the United States.
story:
The bus jolted over the railway tracks, and Laurence's word list nearly slid off her knee. She caught it and kept drilling. The regional bee was in forty minutes, and Sydney had already beaten her twice on "pronunciation," which was frankly humiliating.

"Give me one from the bonus sheet," she said.

Morgan flipped the pages, hunting. "Here. Color. C-O-L-O-U-R."

"That's wrong," Laurence said.

"It is not." Morgan held the sheet like evidence in court. "My cousin lives in Ottawa. She spells it colour every day at school and gets full marks. Your way is the wrong one, or hers is, and it's not hers."

Laurence stared at the two spellings side by side. They couldn't both be right for the same bee, which meant somewhere there was a rule deciding which one counted here, and she didn't know it. She took out her phone, and after a minute of searching while the bus made an abrupt turn that nearly dissolved her grip on the seat, she found it.

"Noah Webster," she read. "In 1828 he published the American Dictionary of the English Language, and he pushed simpler spellings. Color instead of colour. His versions became standard in the United States."

Morgan leaned over. "So in Canada it's still the old way?"

"Looks like it. So your cousin isn't wrong. She's just not spelling for this bee." Laurence set the phone down. "That means the judges here want Webster's version. Color, no u." It was an adaptation, she thought, words changing shape for a new country, and now she knew which shape to use. She wrote it three times on the back of her hand in marker that she hoped wouldn't sweat off.

Morgan was quiet for a stop or two. "I've been telling my cousin her spelling is backwards for two years," Morgan finally said. "I owe her a phone call and probably an apology."

"You can call after I win." Sydney, two rows back, snorted at that, and Laurence turned around in her seat. "You want to test me on it right now?"

"Fine," Sydney said. "Spell it."

Laurence took a breath. "C-O-L-O-R. Color."

Sydney's marker tapped twice against the seat, keeping score.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Every formula in Excel or Google Sheets begins with an equals sign; without it, the cell just shows what was typed as text.
story:
Liam sat at Milania's kitchen table with her laptop open in front of him, a paper list of numbers beside it. They were counting bird sightings for Ms. Teo's science project, and Milania had volunteered her house, her laptop, and her mother's promise of pizza afterward. "You put the numbers in column B," she said, peeling an orange. "Then you make the computer add them."

"I don't know how to make a computer do anything," Liam said. He typed the sightings anyway, ten rows of them, then found the SUM button in the toolbar. The cell filled itself in, and he copied it to the total row the way the menu suggested. Except the cell where the answer should have been didn't show a number. It showed SUM(B2:B10), plain letters sitting there like a label.

"That's not a total," Milania said, leaning over his shoulder. "That's just words." She tried clicking things, then deleted the cell and retyped it by hand, letter by letter, and the same words came back. Liam stared at it. The cell wasn't refusing to add; it was treating his formula like an ordinary sentence. Somewhere in the program there had to be a signal, some mark that told the cell to calculate instead of just display. He thought about the first cell, the one the toolbar had filled in before he copied it, and scrolled up to look.

The original cell started with an equals sign. His retyped version didn't. He deleted his text, typed the equals sign first, then SUM(B2:B10), and the number 47 appeared instantly. "Every formula starts with the equals sign," he said. "Without it, the cell just shows what you typed." Milania slapped the table. "So the equals sign is like raising your hand. It's how the cell knows you're talking to it." They made the bar chart next, and Liam kept adjusting the chart type until the bars came out symmetrical, ten even columns across the screen, one for each day of counting.

Ms. Teo's class would see the chart on Monday, and it looked good, better than good. But Milania's mother called from the hallway that pizza was ready, and Liam understood, watching Milania close the laptop lid over his chart, that the project was shared now, and the grade would be shared too, even though he was the one who had found the equals sign. Her father's colleague had donated the binoculars they'd used, and Milania reminded him of that twice on the way to the kitchen. At the table she slid the biggest slice onto his plate without a word, and Liam, chewing, kept seeing the chart behind his eyes, the bars rising evenly, and hers.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Muscle soreness after an unfamiliar workout is usually worst 24 to 72 hours afterward, which is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
The gym doors opened at 7:20, and the cold air hit Ellie like a wall. "This place is a tundra," Nizar said, rubbing his arms as they walked in. The banners above the far hoop portrayed a snarling wolf, the school mascot, and Ellie looked at it while she laced her shoes. Day one of tryouts. Twelve girls, ten roster spots.

Monday's drills were all new: lunges across the length of the court, defensive slides, box jumps until their legs shook. Ellie went home tired but fine. She texted Nizar that she felt great and went to bed early.

Tuesday morning, she reached the school stairs and stopped halfway up. Her thighs burned so badly she had to take the last steps sideways, one hand on the rail. In the hallway she found Nizar gripping a water fountain, wincing. "I thought I pulled something," he said. "I felt fine yesterday." Ellie lowered herself onto the bench beside him and thought it through. She hadn't fallen, hadn't twisted anything. Every girl who had lunged hard on Monday was walking like a robot today. The two returning players, who had done these drills all last season, moved fine. It wasn't injury. It was something about doing an unfamiliar workout.

"You'd know if you tore something," said Lexy, dropping onto the bench's other end. Lexy was a guard, quick and loud, and she wanted the last spot badly; everyone knew it. "My sister gets it every season. It's called delayed onset muscle soreness. Nobody's immune." She stood, tested her knees with a squat, and winced. "Worst between 24 and 72 hours after. So tomorrow will be even uglier."

Ellie filed that away and made a plan. In the gym, while the others jogged stiffly, she did a long, slow warm-up, then spent the drills choosing her moments instead of chasing every ball. When a loose rebound bounced toward the sideline in the last scrimmage, she didn't sprint for it; she angled, cut off the passing lane, and stole the outlet pass instead. The layup was easy. Mr. González blew his whistle. "Ellie, switch to the first group."

Lexy's head turned at the call. They both knew what the first group meant.

At the end of practice, Mr. González read the names for Wednesday's final session. Ellie heard hers, then Lexy's, then Nizar's, though Nizar only made the manager list and stood there holding the clipboard like it might break. Lexy walked over to Ellie by the door, still moving carefully, and put out her fist. "Last spot tomorrow," she said. "May the least sore legs win."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
Nicolas was sitting on Priya's bedroom floor with her phone balanced on his knee when she yanked it back and stared at the screen like it had insulted her.

"Look at this," she said. "Benson texted me an hour ago, 'Are you still coming to the game?' and I wrote back 'Yeah' and he sent 'Okay.' With a period. Capital O, whole word, period." She dropped the phone on the rug between them. "That's angry. That's the angriest text I've ever gotten in my life."

Nicolas picked it up and read the exchange twice. "It just says okay."

"Exactly. It says okay like a door slamming."

He looked at the little row of messages above it, from earlier that day, when everything seemed fine. Priya had sent Benson a joke about their science teacher, Mr. Clarke, and Benson had replied "haha" with no punctuation at all, then "you coming tonight?" also with nothing. Both of those texts had felt friendly. Only the last one had the period. Nicolas drummed his fingers on the carpet. Maybe it wasn't what Benson said but how it looked on the screen. He thought about how his mom signed her work emails with full sentences and periods, all formal, while his friends never used periods at all.

"Let's test it," he said. "Send me a text. Same word, twice."

Priya grabbed her phone, pulled up Nicolas's contact, and sent "fine" with nothing after it, then "Fine." with the period. Nicolas watched both arrive on his own phone. He read them out loud. The first one sounded like fine. The second one somehow sounded like it had a temper behind it, though it was the same four letters sitting on the same screen.

"I think the period is doing it," he said. "It's not you being paranoid."

He typed "why do periods in texts sound mad" into the search bar, and after a minute of scrolling he found something from Binghamton University. "Listen," he said. "Researchers there did a study in 2016. Messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one." He read it again to make sure he had it right. "Same message, exactly the same, and the one with the period loses."

"So Benson isn't mad at me?"

"He might not be. He might just punctuate like a grown-up." Nicolas thought of Mr. Clarke, who put periods in every text he sent the debate team, even "See you Tuesday." Everyone used to joke about it. Nobody had actually thought Mr. Clarke was furious at all of them.

Priya's worry seemed to evaporate a little, though not entirely. The whole evening hinged on whether she showed up at the game or sat home rereading one punctuation mark. She started typing, deleted it, and typed again. Then she handed the phone to Nicolas so he could see before she hit send.

"Okay!! coming at 7, save me a seat"

She pressed send, and they watched the three dots appear almost immediately.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety; it is a normal stage of development that commonly begins in the second half of a baby's first year.
story:
The note was taped to Ms. Berg's refrigerator, right above the handle where Hudson could not miss it. "Back by nine sharp. Owen's bedtime is eight. There's mac and cheese in the fridge. He's been fussy when we leave, but don't worry. We'll pay you double for the trouble. The Bergs." Hudson read it twice, then looked at Owen, who was eleven months old and banging a spoon on the high chair tray like it owed him money.

The trouble started the second Ms. Berg and her husband picked up their coats. Owen stopped mid-bang. His face crumpled, and the scream that came out of him was enormous, way too big for such a small person. The front door clicked shut behind them and Hudson stood in the kitchen holding a plastic spoon, feeling like the worst babysitter in the history of the world. He checked the note again, as if it might have grown a new paragraph of instructions. It had not. Seven thirty-five. Owen was supposed to be asleep by eight, and at this rate he would still be screaming when he turned forty.

Hudson presumed Owen was hungry or hurt, but the screaming did not sound like either. It sounded like grief. Then he remembered his cousin's baby, and something his aunt had said at Thanksgiving while everyone else was eating pie. He texted his cousin Chanel, who babysat all the time: "Baby losing it when parents left. Normal?" Her reply buzzed back fast: "Totally. It's called separation anxiety. It's a normal stage. Starts around the second half of the first year." Hudson stared at the message. Owen was eleven months old, which fit, and it was normal, which meant it was not his fault. Best of all, Chanel added one more line: "Distraction works. Try something new."

So Hudson tested it. He did not try food, because food was not new. Instead he pulled the colander out of the drawer, put it on his own head like a helmet, and marched around the kitchen table while humming the wrong notes to a song he half knew. Owen hiccupped, sniffled, and stared. Hudson marched the other direction. Owen made a sound halfway between a sob and a laugh. By the third lap the crying was gone entirely, replaced by a squeaky giggle that Hudson would have felt proud of if the colander strap were not cutting into his ears.

Owen fell asleep at 7:58, two minutes to spare, and Hudson lowered him into the crib with the concentration of a bomb technician. Then he sat in the kitchen and ate the mac and cheese alone, and found it tasted like being trusted with something that mattered. When the Bergs came home at nine and pressed the extra money into his hand, Ms. Berg said, "You'll babysit again? Permanently, we hope?" Hudson said yes. He did not mention that he would miss his Saturday nights, or that the colander was now, as far as Owen was concerned, a hat.
